original_value: AbstractAutomated seizure detection from electroencephalography (EEG) would improve the quality of patient care while reducing medical costs, but achieving reliably high performance across patients has proven difficult. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) show promise in addressing this problem, but they are limited by a lack of large labeled training datasets. We propose using imperfect but plentiful archived annotations to train CNNs for automated, real-time EEG seizure detection across patients. While these weak annotations indicate possible seizures with precision scores as low as 0.37, they are commonly produced in large volumes within existing clinical workflows by a mixed group of technicians, fellows, students, and board-certified epileptologists. We find that CNNs trained using such weak annotations achieve Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) values of 0.93 and 0.94 for pediatric and adult seizure onset detection, respectively. Compared to currently deployed clinical software, our model provides a 31% increase (18 points) in F1-score for pediatric patients and a 17% increase (11 points) for adult patients. These results demonstrate that weak annotations, which are sustainably collected via existing clinical workflows, can be leveraged to produce clinically useful seizure detection models.

result.paraphrase: Automated seizure detection from EEG could improve patient care and lower medical costs, yet consistently high performance across patients has been hard to achieve. CNNs are promising for this task, but their effectiveness is constrained by the shortage of large labeled training sets. We therefore propose training CNNs for real-time, cross-patient EEG seizure detection with plentiful but imperfect archived annotations. These weak labels flag possible seizures with precision as low as 0.37, but they are routinely generated in large quantities through existing clinical workflows by technicians, fellows, students, and board-certified epileptologists. Using such weak annotations, we obtain AUROC scores of 0.93 for pediatric seizure onset detection and 0.94 for adult detection. Relative to current clinical software, the model improves F1-score by 31% (18 points) for pediatric patients and 17% (11 points) for adult patients. Overall, the findings show that sustainably collected weak annotations from standard clinical workflows can support clinically useful seizure detection models.
